reviewer: Claude Code (AI assistant). Not an independent human review.
method: Single printed items split from the automatic families of 1770 (long-running ones included; the collection begins in 1770), every item in 3 or more papers counted again by the first 40 words of its opening against every page, papers that comparison missed looked for again and read, a sweep of word-for-word passages shared by 4 or more papers for items the families miss, phrase searches on all 448 pages of 1770 in both transcriptions for every admitted item, and scan checks of each admitted passage, by the thin-year rule (Y-THIN as amended on 23 November 2026: an item printed by more than half of the newspapers that survive for its weeks, and by at least 4, is eligible; items printed by every surviving paper are admitted, the others chosen to cover the months and the kinds of news; in 1770 every eligible item is printed by all four papers)
scan_scope: Each crop covers the excerpt, the opening of the printed item. Long documents were not proofread in full.

new_groups.label: Boston, October 1770: 'At a meeting of the merchants in this town, at the British Coffee-House, it was unanimously voted to alter the Non-Importation Agreement'
new_groups.definition: Printings of a Boston paragraph of October 1770 (dated 11 October in the New-Hampshire Gazette): 'At a meeting of the merchants in this town at the British Coffee-House, it was unanimously voted to alter the Non-Importation Agreement, and to open the importation of goods from Great-Britain, except Teas, and such other articles as are, or may be subject to duties for the purpose of raising a revenue in America.' Other towns' votes on their own agreements, in like words, are other texts.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1770 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Williamsburg, 18 October 1770: 'On Monday the 15th instant, about one o'clock in the morning, departed this life, universally lamented throughout this colony, his Excellency the Right Honourable Norborne Baron de Botetourt'

dispositions_summary.method: The automatic families first printed in 1770 that reach 3 or more papers, long-running ones included, were split into single printed items (story_items.py --long-running, items.json: 32 items printed somewhere; the collection begins in 1770, so there are no families of 1769). Every finder item in 3 or more papers was counted again by the first 40 words of its opening against every page of 1770 in both transcriptions (a page prints the item when it holds at least 18 of the opening's word 5-grams), and texts read from different printings were merged (21 texts). For every text at the bar or one paper short of it, the papers the comparison missed were looked for again on their pages (the best page within the text's weeks) and read. A sweep of seven-word sequences shared by 4 or more papers, over every page, found items the families miss (as X-1803-09); each was read. Every admitted item was then counted by phrase searches of its opening over all 448 pages in both transcriptions, and every hit read (phrase_patterns.json, phrase_hits.json).
dispositions_summary.selection_rule: The thin-year rule (Y-THIN), as amended by the owner on 23 November 2026 (choice B1): an item, counted by its own words, is eligible when it was printed by more than half of the newspapers that survive for its weeks (those with a surviving issue between its first and last printing, and at least in the three weeks from its first printing), and by at least 4; items printed by every newspaper that survives for their weeks are admitted; the other eligible items are chosen to cover the months and the kinds of news; digests are not admitted. 1770 has four papers, so an item reaches the bar only when all four print it: every eligible item is printed by every paper that survives for its weeks, three are admitted, and one that turns on private lives is listed for the owner (R-04); nothing is chosen. The fourth paper, the Massachusetts Spy, survives from 23 August, so no item reaches the bar unless it was still being printed after that day.
dispositions_summary.paper_counting: 1770 has 4 catalogue series, which are 4 papers: the New-Hampshire Gazette and Historical Chronicle (Portsmouth; 50 issues) all year; two Virginia Gazettes, both printed at Williamsburg by different printers, Alexander Purdie and John Dixon (sn84024739; 26 issues, from 15 February) and William Rind (sn84024741; 19 issues, from 25 January); and the Massachusetts Spy (Boston; 17 issues) from 23 August. Papers in print in any three weeks: 1 to 3 before late August; 4 in most windows from late August to December.

counted_item_by_item.Paper counts: The three admitted items and the one listed for the owner are each printed by all four papers, counted by phrase searches of their openings and every hit read; their papers are in the README's table of stories. The items read and below the bar are listed in not_admitted with their counts.
counted_item_by_item.A paragraph in a run of news: The Boston report of the merchants' vote follows a paragraph on the House of Representatives at Cambridge in three papers; the New-Hampshire Gazette prints the vote without it. Each is counted by its own opening: the vote in 4 of 4, the paragraph on the House in 3 of 4.
counted_item_by_item.Notices that only name an item's subject: Proclamations and notices in the Virginia papers that name the governor, Lord Botetourt, are not counted with the report of his death.

for_user_decision.The floor of four papers before 23 Augus: As built: before 23 August only three papers survive (in January and February fewer), so no item printed only then reaches the bar of 4; the town of Boston's account of the night of 5 March 1770, and its committee to the Lieutenant Governor, are printed by all three papers that survive for their weeks and are below the bar, as is the King's speech of 9 January. All three admitted items were first printed in October.
for_user_decision.A paragraph on a nobleman's private life: As built (R-04): a one-sentence London paragraph on what 'appeared upon a late trial' about a nobleman's mistresses since his marriage is printed by every paper that survives for its weeks, but it turns on private lives, so it is listed for the owner, without names (it names no one). If the owner sees it as a public matter, it is admitted by the rule's first part.
